title: Critics Say Main Vaapas Aaunga Is Imtiaz Ali's Best Work. The Box Office Didn't Get the Memo.
excerpt: Diljit Dosanjh and Naseeruddin Shah deliver a devastating Partition love story backed by A.R. Rahman — and it opened to just ₹1.15 crore.
body:
The morning after Main Vaapas Aaunga opened in theatres, the numbers told one story and the critics told an entirely different one. ₹1.15 crore on Day 1. Eleven percent occupancy. A start so muted it wouldn't make noise in a library. And yet, the reviews read like a standing ovation.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=PRUTWluKRW8

Imtiaz Ali — the man who made a generation believe in love stories set at train stations and highway dhabas — has delivered what multiple critics are calling his most mature, most devastating film. Not Jab We Met. Not Tamasha. Not Rockstar. This one. A 167-minute partition drama about a 95-year-old man who wants to cross a border that was drawn through his childhood, and the grandson who flies from England to make it happen.

"Possibly Imtiaz Ali's best work and one of the most effective love stories in recent Hindi cinema." — DNA India
"The album is eight tracks deep, with "Kya Kamaal Hai" sung by Diljit himself becoming the emotional anchor."

That grandson is played by Diljit Dosanjh — who, less than a week ago, was onstage at the FIFA World Cup opening ceremony in Toronto, and is now onscreen as Nirvair Grewal, a British-settled Punjabi navigating the emotional wreckage of 1947 through the eyes of someone who never lived it. Opposite him, Naseeruddin Shah plays Ishar Singh Grewal at 95, a man whose body has slowed but whose memory of a lost love refuses to quiet down. Vedang Raina plays the young Ishar, carrying the film's most harrowing sequences with a rawness that feels earned, and Sharvari doubles as both the past and the present — Afsana in 1947, Jiya in 2026.

https://www.instagram.com/reel/DZbyZMjhFu8/

The partition genre in Indian cinema has a long, complicated history. Most films go for scale — the trains, the fires, the masses fleeing. Ali does something quieter and far harder. He stays inside one family's memory. The camera, handled by Sylvester Fonseca, doesn't look at partition. It looks at what partition did to the people who survived it and then spent seventy-eight years pretending they hadn't.

"Imtiaz Ali and Naseeruddin Shah turn memory and longing into cinema that cannot be missed." — Hindustan Times

A.R. Rahman's score is the kind that doesn't announce itself — it seeps. The album is eight tracks deep, with "Kya Kamaal Hai" sung by Diljit himself becoming the emotional anchor. "Maskara," a peppy, playful duet between Nilanjana Ghosh Dastidar and Vedang Raina, breaks the heaviness at exactly the right moment. The lyrics, penned by the ever-reliable Irshad Kamil, find that Imtiaz Ali sweet spot between poetry and plain speech.

Here's what makes this sting, though: the film is struggling precisely because of what makes it special. At ₹70 crore, it's not cheap. On the same day, it faced Kangana Ranaut's Bharat Bhhagya Viddhaata, Manoj Bajpayee's Governor, and a surprise attack from Mimoh Chakraborty's Haunted 3D — which, against all odds and reason, actually outperformed every new Hindi release on opening day.

The Bollywood Hungama verdict put it plainly: the film appeals to "a niche, urban multiplex audience." The Hollywood Reporter India called it "a partition-era story worth falling for." The question now is whether word-of-mouth — which is strong, emotional, and deeply personal — can push this past a weekend that needs to hit at least ₹6 crore to give the film any chance at survival.

Where to Watch for the Diaspora

For NRI audiences in the US, UK, and Canada, Main Vaapas Aaunga is playing in select theatres through Birla Studios' international distribution. This is the kind of film that hits different when you're watching it 8,000 miles from Punjab. The partition isn't just history — for many in the diaspora, it's a grandparent's story that was never fully told. If your family came from what's now Pakistan, bring tissues. If they didn't, bring them anyway.

This marks the second collaboration between Imtiaz Ali and Diljit Dosanjh after the magnificent Amar Singh Chamkila (2024). Where Chamkila was electric and visceral, Main Vaapas Aaunga is its opposite — slow, tender, aching. Both films prove that this is one of the most exciting actor-director partnerships in Hindi cinema right now. The box office may not agree yet, but the cinema absolutely does.
